title: Integration discovery - Meridian Logistics
summary: Discovery focused on integration options (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private), SDK support, LangChain/LlamaIndex adapters, gateway/proxy patterns, rate limits/quotas, and observability hooks. Customer has a production microservices platform on AWS EKS, security requirements for audit logs and KMS, and needs low-latency inference for routing and document summarization. Next steps agreed: share SDK examples, LangChain adapter notes, rate-limit matrix, and schedule a short latency benchmark with a sample workload.
topics: Current infra: AWS EKS, Kafka, Postgres, internal API gateway
LangChain and LlamaIndex connectors and best practices
Gateway/proxy pattern for request routing and auth
Rate limits, quotas, and burst policies for Dedicated vs Hosted
Observability hooks: per-route metrics, token-level cost, tracing
Security: KMS/HSM, SOC2, VPC/private deployment questions
Pilot scope and success criteria (latency, cost, data controls)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-05-18 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Alex Morgan (Redwood AE), Priya Singh (Redwood SE), Tom Reyes (Meridian CTO), Leila Wu (Platform Eng), Diego Martinez (Head of ML), Sara Bennett (DevOps)

Summary/Notes (auto): 
- High-level: evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private for inference across routing and document summarization workloads.
- Primary constraints: sub-200ms tail latency for small prompts, strict audit logs, customer-managed keys, prefer VPC peering for dedicated private routing.
- Actionables at end.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Morgan: hey everyone thanks for joining, this is Alex from Redwood, i'm the AE on the account, with me is priya our se and hugo on solutions, hows everyone doing?
[00:06] Tom Reyes: good thanks alex, excited to dig in today, we wanted to cover integration patterns and what the lift looks like for each deployment mode.
[00:12] Priya Singh: great, we'll try to focus on SDKs, langchain/llamaindex adapters, gateway/proxy options, and also rate limiting and observability. maybe start with your current stack?
[00:20] Leila Wu: sure, we're on AWS, EKS for microservices, kafka for events, postgres for metadata. most of our services talk through an internal api gateway. we currently run smaller models in-house for routing but it's inconsistent.
[00:29] Diego Martinez: our main use case is real-time routing (parcel routing heuristics) and doc summarization for customer support  both need fast responses, routing under 200ms ideally.
[00:36] Sara Bennett: and we have strict requirements around audit logs and encryption at rest, we use AWS KMS and an HSM for some keys.
[00:42] Alex Morgan: thanks, that helps. quick high level: hosted gives fastest time to value, dedicated gives predictable throughput and isolation, private gives you the control we discussed (VPC or on-prem). for integration lift  our SDKs (python/js) are small wrappers over the REST API and support streaming, function calling and structured outputs.
[01:01] Priya Singh: to add, we have reference langchain connectors and a llamaindex loader we've open-sourced  they map seamlessly to our streaming and tool-calling features. if you're already using langchain, it's usually a few lines to swap the backend.
[01:12] Leila Wu: is that adapter maintained by redwood? how cutting-edge is it for async streaming?
[01:16] Priya Singh: yes maintained by our integrations team, supports both sync and async for python, and handles incremental streaming tokens for llm chains. we also publish examples showing prefix cache and using our sdk with langchain agents.
[01:26] Tom Reyes: good  for compliance we need audit logs and token-level cost breakdowns, plus the ability to force all traffic through our gateway. can hosted meet that?
[01:33] Alex Morgan: hosted provides detailed usage and token-level costing in the console and api access to logs; for stricter controls we recommend either Dedicated with private networking or Private (VPC)  both can be configured to route through your gateway/proxy and use customer-managed KMS.
[01:45] Diego Martinez: what does "route through our gateway" look like  do we maintain a proxy that calls redwood, or do you provide a sidecar?
[01:51] Hugo Park: common pattern is an internal proxy (sidecar or central gateway) that handles auth, request enrichment, and rate limiting. you can either call Redwood's hosted endpoints directly from your gateway, or with Dedicated/Private we can peer into your VPC so the traffic stays private. we also support customer-side token exchange so no long-lived credentials are stored in services.
[02:08] Sara Bennett: how about rate limits  we have bursts during peak delivery windows; want to avoid throttling that blocks the pipeline.
[02:14] Priya Singh: for hosted we enforce per-account rate limits and quotas; they can be raised with commitments. Dedicated gives you reserved throughput and configurable burst policies, and Private is fully under your control for autoscaling. we can share a rate-limit matrix that maps RPS and token throughput to instance counts.
[02:28] Tom Reyes: ok, we'd like to see numbers for a 500 RPS small-prompt workload and a 20 RPS long-context summarization workload; can you run a benchmark?
[02:36] Alex Morgan: yes we can do a short latency/cost benchmark using your sample prompts. typical next step is a 1-2 hour test on Dedicated or Hosted with instrumented telemetry so you get p50/p95/p99 and token costs.
[02:46] Leila Wu: about observability: we use datadog and opentelemetry  what hooks do you expose?
[02:51] Priya Singh: we emit per-request metrics (latency, tokens_in/out, model, route) and have tracing integrations for opentelemetry. we also provide per-route dashboards in the console, and an exportable stream of audit logs S3 or via webhook. many customers ingest those into datadog or their SIEM.
[03:07] Diego Martinez: do you expose kv cache stats? we want to see hit rates for prefix caching because we plan to use repetition across requests.
[03:13] Hugo Park: yes, cache hit/miss rates are surfaced and you can configure prefix caching policies; we also do automatic kv-cache warmup for common prompt prefixes in Dedicated to reduce cold-start latency.
[03:23] Tom Reyes: what about model pinning and rollouts? we need to test model variants for quality/regressions.
[03:28] Priya Singh: the console supports model version pinning per-route, canary rollouts, and automatic fallback policies. and we have eval hooks so you can tie regressions to a prompt set and get alerts.
[03:37] Leila Wu: integration lift question: what does the python sdk look like for langchain  is there an example repo we can clone?
[03:41] Priya Singh: yes, i'll drop links  small python example (10-20 lines) showing LangChain LLM wrapper, stream handling, and a llamaindex loader example. we also have a node example for our SDK.
[03:49] Tom Reyes: security  SOC2 is fine, but we need a contract clause about data retention and ability to purge logs on request.
[03:55] Alex Morgan: we have SOC2 and can commit to retention windows per your account policy; for Private deployments retention is fully in your control. we'll share the security pack and legal boilerplate.
[04:04] Diego Martinez: on latency  you mentioned kernel selection and quantization  for small prompts are you recommending quantized models? they sometimes increase latency.
[04:11] Priya Singh: good callout. quantized models reduce memory footprint and cost, but depending on kernel and GPU they can slightly increase token latency. for sub-200ms needs we usually recommend a tuned FP16 pipeline or quantization-profiled models with optimized kernels; we can test both in benchmarks.
[04:26] Leila Wu: what about SDK rate limit handling  if we hit a 429 do you return retry-after? do you provide client-side helpers?
[04:33] Hugo Park: yes, our SDKs surface 429 with retry-after headers and include exponential backoff helpers. for Dedicated we also offer queueing policies and burst bursts  so you can accept bursts and have them processed as capacity frees up.
[04:46] Tom Reyes: timeline: we want to decide in 3-4 weeks. success criteria: p95 latency under 250ms for routing, cost target under $0.0005/token for the routing workload, and ability to route through our gateway with KMS.
[04:58] Alex Morgan: solid. we'll: share SDK examples + langchain/llamaindex repos, a rate-limit matrix, security docs, and propose a short benchmark plan.
[05:08] Leila Wu: can you also share a sample observability dashboard so our SREs can validate metrics?
[05:12] Priya Singh: yes, we'll export a dashboard json for datadog and a sample opentelemetry config.
[05:18] Tom Reyes: perfect thanks, any final Qs?
[05:21] Sara Bennett: one last  for the private option, what's the on-prem packaging like? operator, helm chart?
[05:27] Hugo Park: we provide a helm chart + operator and an air-gapped bundle for on-prem with docs for HSM/KMS integrations.
[05:34] Alex Morgan: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the artifacts and a proposed date for the benchmark, i'll be your main contact.
[05:41] Tom Reyes: thanks alex, priya. bye all.

End of transcript.
